How did Estonia and Latvia manage to win a war against Russia and Germany during the years 1918-1920?

An older post, but I'll answer anyway. The short version is, it's got a lot to do with the bigger picture. Germany was already on the verge of losing WWI, and Russia was collapsing into Civil War. It was also a completely different era for warfare. Conscripts and volunteers with rifles were still the primary combat force for any nation. The tanks and aircraft of the era were largely irrelevant in Baltic campaign. Naval superiority already belonged to the Western Entente. Massed heavy artillery, as seen on the western front, could not be effectively deployed and repositioned in the more mobile tactical conditions in the East, so artillery was limited to light, direct-fire field guns. In other words, the few military technologies that only major nations could afford were irrelevant to warfare on the eastern front, so there was no insurmountable technological advantage for the Germans. Russia was already a second rate power when it came to military technology and doctrine.

Beyond that, there was also support from Britain, providing guns and naval support. And Finland providing volunteer soldiers. On the the German front we weren't really fighting the regular army of the German Empire, but rather a militia formed and led by the Baltic German nobility, and armed by the German Empire, so training and equipment-wise, they were essentially in the same position as Estonian and Latvian forces. Their supply was eventually cut off by British blockade and advances by Poland in their civil war. The Soviets were in the throes of their own Civil War, and had many other fronts to deal with; the White Russians were nominally allied to the Baltics. Peace in the Baltics happened largely for two reasons: firstly because the Soviets wanted to close the front and make Leningrad more secure. Secondly, the Baltic States were open to negotiating with the Soviets, was because the British saw the region as a legitimate part of a non-Communist Russian Empire, so we really had no reason to support the Whites any more than necessary to achieve our own independence.

Three weeks ago I started a new job. I went from working in an office for a few years to getting back into kitchens. I decided if I'm going to go back into cooking again (did it for 8 years previously) that I want to work at the best place that serves not only amazing tasting food, but sourced well. I got a job at a local joint where the chef gets a lot of stuff from local farmers. He knows their stories, he knows the animals' diet, he knows this food. He has also worked for big name chefs like Michel Richard and Thomas Keller - titans of cooking. He owns a small house converted to hotel/fine dining restaurant in my small town. The dining room seats few and 25-30 people is a "busy night". Contrary to popular belief, there is not a lot of money in fine dining.

Anyway, I was amazed by this guy and hugely intimidated by him as well. The kitchen in small, so I knew there would be a lot riding on me if I joined the team. Not to mention that this is the fanciest food I would have ever cooked. After day 2 I came home and basically cried. I am on a salary and the first few days I worked 12 hour shifts. I did the math and I would be making less than minimum wage at this rate. I don't get to see my wife and child as often as I did previously and I felt like I had made a huge mistake. On top of this - I don't want to be a chef. I love food, but I don't desire cooking for the rest of my life even though I am really good at it.

The next morning I spent applying to different jobs. Anything with benefits, good hours, etc. In a small town - that's not a lot. So that day I go into work and stick it out, feeling cheated. The food was great, the atmosphere was great, but the pay and hours just plain suck. That night I'm cleaning up and the chef is starting on prep for the next day. He asked me how I felt about the job and.....like a mad man, I told him. For a chef (and boss I worked under for all of 3 days) he was not only understanding, but helpful. We had a long talk about ways to work around this, how to shorten my hours to get more bang for my buck, and other jobs he can hook me up with.

He is honestly the nicest chef/boss I have ever met. There is so much honesty it's unreal. He just wants to play with food and make this community great. He wants to showcase the food of local farmers and he only pays himself $15K a year. I never met a chef that pays me more than himself - and he works twice the hours. The kitchen has a garden I can play around in too. This past week was "restaurant week" (a promotional thing) and for a place where 30 covers is a lot of people - we did 40-60 every night. I worked 12-14 hours shifts every day. I'm beat, but I feel really good. I'm sticking with it and the chef is very impressed by me, almost favoring me over the other cooks. He wants to find me a job where I can have 9-5 hours, benefits, and somehow still work with food. And fuck, we're going to a mushroom farm in a few days just to take a tour. He compliments my skills daily and told me "I see you as this super-dad who can cook and garden in his free time, but also works at a job he loves - and I want to help get you there." Oh, and he's so impressed by me he is increasing my pay.

My life went from grueling office work to exciting, rewarding, and challenging. I feel so much more human now. I know I need to live as an ant before I can live as a grasshopper.
3 weeks ago I wanted to quit my new job, today I am so thankful I stuck with it.
